questions.q: Why does this lesson say Salesforce capability upgrades are usually a recurring cost rather than a one-time purchase?
options: Because most capability add-ons, like Salesforce Shield or a higher license tier, are priced per user and bill every year, whether or not the capability is fully used
Because Salesforce prohibits one-time capability purchases by policy
Because capability upgrades always decrease in price every year automatically
Because Salesforce only sells capability upgrades as part of a multi-year contract with no annual option
questions.explain: Shield and license-tier upgrades are per-user, recurring costs -- if a user with a full CRM license never actually uses that extra capability, the org is still paying full price for it every billing cycle.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as 'over-provisioning' in the cost-vs-capability tradeoff?
options: Buying the cheaper, lower-capability option to save money immediately
Buying a more capable license or add-on 'to be safe' without a concrete, current plan to use it, locking in a recurring cost for capability that may sit unused
Measuring current usage before making a licensing decision
Purchasing additional sandboxes only after a documented need for parallel development arises
questions.explain: Over-provisioning is treated as its own real failure mode in this lesson, not the automatically safe choice -- it locks in ongoing spend for capability that may never get used, money that could fund something the org actually needs now.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as 'under-provisioning,' and what risk does it carry?
options: Buying more licenses than current headcount requires
Choosing Salesforce Shield for every user in the org

Buying the cheaper, lower-capability option to save money now, risking hitting a wall later -- such as API limits throttling a live integration -- and needing an emergency, more expensive fix under time pressure
Scheduling sandbox refreshes on a disciplined cadence
questions.explain: Under-provisioning saves money now but risks discovering the gap at the worst possible moment, needing a rushed and costlier fix -- the savings were real, and so is the risk.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the root cause shared by both over-provisioning and under-provisioning?
options: Both are caused by a lack of available AppExchange packages
Both are caused exclusively by Salesforce's pricing model changing without notice
Both only happen in orgs with fewer than 50 users
Both come from picking a capability level based on what sounds appropriately cautious or appropriately lean, rather than measured current usage and a specific near-term forecast
questions.explain: The lesson frames both failure modes as stemming from the same mistake: deciding based on a feeling of caution or leanness instead of a concrete, named, near-term use case.

questions.q: What criterion does this lesson give for deciding whether to buy ahead of strict present need for a given capability?
options: Whether the cost of discovering the gap too late (for example, retrofitting encryption onto years of existing data) is much higher than the cost of paying for headroom now, versus a capability that's cheap and fast to add later
Always buy ahead of need, regardless of the capability, since it is never risky to over-provision
Whether a competitor organization has already purchased the same capability
Whether the capability was mentioned in a Salesforce product keynote
questions.explain: The lesson draws a real distinction: capabilities that are catastrophically expensive or risky to retrofit later justify buying ahead of strict need, while capabilities that are cheap and fast to add later (like one more sandbox or a few extra seats) don't need to be bought on spec.
